title: Tag Validator
statement: Decide whether the string `code` is a well-formed snippet of a small tag language, returning `true` or `false`. Read `code` from left to right with these rules: - The whole of `code` must be exactly one **closed tag**: a start tag ``, then its content, then the end tag `` with the identical name. Nothing may come before or after it. - A tag **name** is valid only if it consists of 1 to 9 upper-case letters. Whenever `<` or ``; if there is no later `>`, or the name is invalid, `code` is invalid. - Content may hold any characters, nested closed tags and cdata sections, but every `<` in it must start either a valid tag or a cdata section, and start and end tags must pair up properly nested (`` is invalid). - A **cdata section** opens with `` after it. Everything between those markers is plain text and is never parsed as tags. Cdata may appear only inside a tag's content.
constraints: code contains only English letters, digits, '<', '>', '/', '!', '[', ']', '.' and spaces
notes:
## Intuition Tags nest like brackets, so a stack of open tag names checks the pairing: a start tag pushes its name and an end tag must pop the same name. The extra rules are about *reading*: cdata is skipped as a block, any other `<` must form a valid tag, and the outer tag must close exactly at the end of `code`. (A slower idea, used as the brute force, hides cdata and then repeatedly deletes innermost `...` pairs until one remains.) ## Approach 1. Walk `code` with index `i` and a `stack` of open names. 2. If `i > 0` and the `stack` is empty, the outer tag has already closed (or never opened), so anything more is invalid. 3. Inside a tag, ``; with no `]]>` the code is invalid. 4. Any other `<` is a tag. Note whether it is `closing`, read the `name` up to the next `>`, and reject it if it is missing or not 1 to 9 upper-case letters. 5. An end tag must pop exactly `name`; a start tag pushes it. Then jump past the `>`. 6. Any other character is plain text, allowed only inside a tag. 7. At the end the `stack` must be empty. ## Example 1, step by step `
` pushes `DIV`. The text `This is the first line ` is skipped one character at a time. ``, so `
` is never parsed. `
` pops `DIV`, `i` reaches the end with an empty stack, and the answer is `true`. ## Complexity - Time: O(n): every character is passed once, by a step or a jump. - Space: O(n) for the stack of names. ## Pitfalls - A root that closes early, as in ``, must fail: check for an empty stack before each step. - Only the first `]]>` ends a cdata section; later ones are ordinary text. - `<` inside text is never harmless: ` < ` reads the name ` ` or `>` that ends the current piece | | `closing` | whether the tag is an end tag | | `start` | index where the tag name begins | | `name` | the tag's name |

narration.4: Read the code from left to right; i always points at the next unread character.
narration.5: An empty stack after the start means the outer tag has already closed, so nothing more may follow.
narration.8: Inside a tag, a cdata opener starts a block that is never parsed.
narration.9: The block ends at the first ]]> after the opener.
narration.13: Jump past the whole cdata section.
narration.14: Any other < must begin a start or end tag.
narration.17: The tag name runs up to the next >.
narration.22: A name must be 1 to 9 upper-case letters.
narration.26: An end tag must close the most recently opened tag with the same name.
narration.30: A start tag opens a new level of nesting.
narration.33: Plain text before the first tag is outside any closed tag.
narration.36: Plain text inside a tag is allowed; move on one character.
narration.39: Every opened tag must have been closed.
